Q: Looking for a pattern to add information in any output stream that could be used later by another tool A:

Just keep in mind that the ostream in question is std::cout which is not destructed until the end of the program, so the callback won't be called for that stream until the program is exiting. Thus cout will stay in the table for a long time, which may or may not be desired depending on the intended use of the table.

Also, note that using iword() is sticky, so if one call to tostr() specifies a precision and the next call does not, the previous precision still gets applied to the output.

Another thing to think about is if the OP later decides that they want to create separate << operators for tostr_sep, tostr_lbrace, and tostr_rbrace as well. You can't store all of those values in the stream's iword() storage. You would have to hold the values in a custom object that is stored in the stream's pword() storage instead, but then you are back to dealing with the lifetime issue of that object. At least here, the callback becomes useful, since the same object can be reused for multiple calls to tostr().

Regardless of how the code decides to save its format settings, I would probably just have tostr() cleanup after itself after writing to the ostream. This is similar to some standard I/O manipulators whose values get reset after each write, such as std::setw.

Q: Searching for strings in multiple text files and outputting matched lines to a CSV A:

Maybe first use print() to see what code is executed and what you have in variables. Sometimes it is called "print debuging" and it can help to understand what can be the problem.

First problem can be open('output.csv', 'w') which deletes previous content.
You may have to do one of this:

  • first get all data and open csv only once (after for-loop) to write all data at once.
  • open csv before for-loop and keep it open all time. And close afer loop. Or put all loop in with open(...) as ...:.
  • use append mode a instead of write mode w and it will not remove previous content when you reopen file. Eventually you may run w at the beginning to make sure file doesn't have results from previous execution.
